Infographics

Three one-page data stories, built entirely in R. Each takes official data, finds one clear message, and builds the page around it. Under each one: the choices behind the charts, and what I would change next time.

Vietnam’s boom has bypassed its northern mountains

Data: General Statistics Office of Vietnam and World Bank · GDP per person, multidimensional poverty and travel turnover, 63 provinces, 2016–2022

Behind the chart

The story. Vietnam’s economy has grown about 7% a year, but the national average hides where the growth went. One page shows who has been left behind, and whether tourism reaches them.

One map, two indicators. A bivariate map shows GDP per person and poverty together, so the reader sees where they overlap without comparing two maps. It was also my first bivariate map: I used this project to learn the technique.

A treemap for tourism. The point is the size of the gap. Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi fill most of the space (78%); the five poorest provinces (0.08%) almost disappear.

A dumbbell for change. Only the five poorest provinces and Vietnam as a whole: the places that need most help, against the benchmark. It stops in 2021 because the poverty measure changed in 2022.

Handling the data

  • Cleaned hidden characters in province names before joining to the map.
  • Six provinces with no 2022 poverty rate are shown in grey, not dropped.
  • Tourism is recorded where companies are registered, which favours big cities.

What I’d do differently

  • Add an annotated legend to make the bivariate map easier to read.
  • Note the 2022 change in the poverty measure on the map itself.

Asked to breastfeed for six months, paid for three

Data: UNICEF global database on infant and young child feeding (surveys in 96 countries, 2010–2022) · World Bank paid leave laws (189 economies, 2023)

Behind the chart

The story. WHO recommends six months of feeding only breast milk. The typical country pays mothers about three months of leave. The page puts the recommendation and the reality side by side.

A calendar of the first year. Everyone understands weeks. The six-month recommendation and the 14 paid weeks sit on the same time scale, so the gap shows without any axis: the paid-leave line simply stops halfway.

Filled weeks. Each week is filled to the share of babies of that age fed only breast milk. Read together, the weeks work as a bar chart: 60% at first, 24% by months 4–5.

A typical country. Both figures are medians, so a few countries with very long leave don’t pull the picture up.

Handling the data

  • Two sources covering different countries: the page compares a typical country in each.
  • The data don’t show that leave ending causes the drop, and the page says so.
  • Leave laws miss many informal workers, so the real gap is likely larger.

What I’d do differently

  • Calculate paid leave for the same 96 countries as the breastfeeding data.
  • Show the spread between countries, not only the median.

Hong Kong’s summers are getting hotter and longer

Data: Hong Kong Observatory, via data.gov.hk · daily maximum and mean temperature and daily rainfall, 1953–2025

Behind the chart

The story. About 13 very hot days a year in the 1950s, about 52 since 2020. Not only more hot days, but a hot season that starts earlier and ends later.

Every day in one picture. The radial calendar fits more than 26,000 days into a small space. The red band grows thicker (more hot days) and wider (a longer season): a bar chart shows the first, not the second.

The official definition. A very hot day is 33 °C or more, the Observatory’s own threshold, so the figures can be compared with what it publishes.

Not only heat. Total rainfall has no trend, but the wettest day of the year got much heavier: 162 mm in the 1950s, 265 mm in the 2020s.

Handling the data

  • 1953–2025 only: every year in that range has complete records.
  • “Trace” rain (under 0.05 mm) counted as zero.
  • One urban station: part of the warming may come from the city around it.

What I’d do differently

  • Outer rings are longer, so recent years look bigger. Add a flat heatmap alongside.
  • Check the colours for colour-blind readers.
